title: Don't we just love his movies

commenti.body: He’s definitely one of the foremost auteurs in modern cinema. His style is instantly recognizable and endlessly watchable, though I’m not a huge fan of his B-Movie endeavors. My favorites are Inglorious Basterds and Django Unchained. I had qualms with Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, but his restraint makes me interested in his final film.

From a quality perspective I think he shouldve surrounded himself with more people who could say: «hold up, maybe not. Isnt there any less insane way to achieve this?».

But his style is snappy, and he has cool characters. Not always the deepest, but they are intriguing to watch how they interract.

On the other hand it is in some refreshing to see movies that indulge themselves so much in what they want to be with little care if it is maybe too much

Jackie Brown and Once Upon a Time in Hollywood are the only films of his that I respect. The latter, I believe, is his best work and a masterpiece. 

Reservoir Dogs and Pulp Fiction, which I loved upon their release, seemed surprisingly substandard in more recent viewings. 

I don't really care for his other movies. However, I must admit, the opening scene of Inglourious Basterds is tight and great. But in my opinion, nothing else he has made matches that intensity and sharpness.

First off, I like Tarantinofilms.  I also dislike them.  I even dislike the ones I like.  Funny how that works.  

His movies (and I'm not saying this is good or bad) are unrealistic.  Violence and suffering almost always take on a cartoonish look, an over-exagerrated or even physically impossible stance.  His movies are like comic strips.  A person gets hurt, a big bump swells, then they're back to normal.  Not literally, but such is the impression of his films of a strong unreality.  Perhaps most importantly...an unreality that disguises itself as a reality.  

He's a very extroverted filmmaker.  Everything about his movies are talkative, busy, and action packed.  His characters are surfacey and lack complexity, though they're interesting to watch...to LOOK at.  He's very sensory attuned, and certainly prizes a good explosion or overdose rather than any sort of philosophical or poetic expression that might bring such situations further.  He occupies that area quite well.  He's like the polar opposite of Bergman or Tarkovsky (I'd love to know what his opinions are on directors such as them) but he's better than his matches, people like Michael Bay.  He brings a bit of odyssey and imagination to mainstream blockbusters where others simply fail.  

The thing that strikes me most about his movies is that they're total artifice.  Yet, people engage with them as though they're depictions of reality.  In this way, the average Tarantino fan has something in common with a child watching cartoons.  And once again, I think that's fine, but certainly a wow factor that I only realized later in life.  I saw Pulp Fiction when I was 6, amidst Bugs Bunny and other similar features.  To me it's not a long shot to say his movies are just hyper-loonytoon worlds.  

Yeah I like the guy, and don't.  One hand gives a big thumbs up while the other says 'stop.'  I think few filmmakers make me feel that way.  Now I want to go watch some Tarantino films.

My feelings are that he has greatness in him but often gets in his own way. He has made some great movies, specifically Pulp Fiction and Jackie Brown. But I find his historical fiction to be often sophomoric. The re-writing of history in the endings of Basterds and Hollywood both made me roll my eyes. And it’s because I know he thinks it’s *sOoOo* cool, alright? But contrast that crap with something like the complexity of Sam Jackson’s character in Django, which is just extraordinary in its writing and directing, as well as maybe coaxing out Jackson’s career best performance. Pulp Fiction and Jackie Brown aren’t without their flaws, but I’ve said they were made by Quentin Tarantino and every movie he’s made since has been made by QUENTIN TARANTINO, and I preferred the first guy.

I prefer Pulp Fiction’s Dialogue and Pacing. There was that bit of humour in it that made it so  much fun to watch. Kill Bill marked his change away from that. It started to feel more like the characters are lecturing at me rather than interacting with each other at times.

Someone who shares my opinion. 

Actually upon watching, OUATIH, i felt even Jackie brown felt more forced, in the sense that, JB as QT himself told, was a pseudo mature endeavour.

It's with OUATIH that his maturity is felt in a more natural way. The characters seem to have aged the way QT himself has, and he himself seems to have had changing priorities.

Even the structure of the film seems to be parodying the typical QT film, but then subverts it do beautifully.

My most favourite of his.

Sad that he wouldn't be continuing in this style for a long time.

>Sad that he wouldn't be continuing in this style for a long time.

Do you mean this because he won't be making any more movies?

Also, If you haven't read it, “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” (the book) is a super fun read and extends the dimensions of the movie, making it even better.

Ya

According to him, he'll be making only one more movie, so that's a bummer.

I had heard about it, but havent gotten around to reading it.👍

I have to agree. It’s a strange dichotomy where to more films I watch and the more directors I check out, the less I like Tarantino’s work as a whole. 

Which is fine because it turns out I enjoy much different things than what Tarantino enjoys. I saw a quote from him dismissing A Clockwork Orange. He said something how he he believes Kubrick only made the movie so he could film the few minutes of violence. 

To me this shows a lack of depth from Tarantino’s psyche and what he prioritizes in film, Communicating violence to the audience. Personally Haneke seems to be better at that, and simultaneously able to criticize the violence and make the viewer feel squirmy for it. 

Lynch, haneke, Von Trier,  Altman are all much better film makers than Tarantino. In terms of blockbuster film makers I think Nolan and Scorsese are better. 

That being said Once Upon a Time in Hollywood actually kicked me off into enjoying films. It started me into criterion because I wanted to watch the movies that are referenced in the film. I do still love Tarantino but I just ultimately think some of his films lack a maturity. For example some of his “extended cameos” are really goofy in hindsight. I’m not even talking about his n word scene in Pulp Fiction, that role he wrote for himself in Django is laughable.
